records.sourceFile: Reference Values for Hydration Biomarkers - Optimizing Athletic Performance and Recovery.pdf

paper.citation: Armstrong LE, Stearns RL, Huggins RA, Sekiguchi Y, Mershon AJ, Casa DJ. Reference Values for Hydration Biomarkers: Optimizing Athletic Performance and Recovery. Open Access Journal of Sports Medicine. 2025;16:31-50.
paper.abstract: The authors compile reference values for body mass change, urine specific gravity and thirst rating from 16 field studies across competitions, training, weight-making and daily life. They propose using these values alongside an individual's own baselines within a personalized hydration plan.
paper.tldr: When athletes lost body mass during exercise, urine specific gravity and thirst rating rose in every compiled field study, so a combination of these three measures is more useful than one threshold. Use the compiled values as a comparison point against each athlete's own baseline, not as a diagnostic cut-off.
paper.methods: Narrative review with a described search of PubMed and Google Scholar (English, full-text, peer-reviewed, adult participants, to May 1, 2024) plus reference-list checks. From 3,224 records, 385 full texts were assessed and 16 field studies were included. Values were tabulated for outdoor competition and training (Table 1), weight-making in combat sports (Table 2), exertional hyponatremia cases (Table 3), morning versus afternoon free-living (Table 4) and 24-hour water restriction (Table 5). Correlations were calculated on group means from Tables 1 and 2.
paper.findings: Table 1 shows body mass losses of 0.1% to 2.7% across outdoor events, with urine specific gravity and thirst rating rising in every study. For example, collegiate American football players lost 1.2% body mass with urine specific gravity from 1.020 to 1.024 and thirst from 4 to 6. In combat sports, a 48-hour weight-cut in judo lost 4.9% body mass with urine specific gravity from 1.014 to 1.026. In 14 men on 24 hours of water restriction, body mass fell 2.1% and urine specific gravity rose from 1.020 to 1.030, with thirst rating on a visual analog scale rising from 55 to 88. Body mass change correlated with urine specific gravity (r = 0.50, P = .013) and thirst (r = 0.68, P = .001). Two cyclists with exertional hyponatremia showed biomarker responses that differed from the comparison group.
paper.limitations: The paper has no separate limitations section. The reference values come from 16 small studies, and the authors do not pool them statistically beyond the group-mean correlations. Several studies did not report standard deviations, thirst was measured on two different scales, and combat sport data were limited to a few studies. The correlations are calculated across group means, which may overstate agreement within individuals. The search was limited to two databases and English-language articles.
paper.practicalImplications: Staff can record body mass, urine specific gravity and a thirst rating before and after sessions and compare changes with the ranges in Tables 1 to 5 and with each athlete's own baseline. The authors advise measuring at consistent times of day and seeking medical review if body mass rises or urine specific gravity stays unusually low after exercise.
paper.athleteDev: The compiled values can help coaches and athletes build an individual hydration plan from measured sweat rate and event length. The paper does not test whether any hydration plan improves performance.
paper.rtp: Not applicable. The review does not study injury, rehabilitation or return to play.
